items.q: What makes Kafka a log rather than a traditional message queue?

options.t: Records survive being read, so many consumers replay independently
options.why: Right. A queue deletes on delivery; a log keeps records for its retention window, and each consumer group tracks its own position. That one difference is why replay, multiple readers, and backfills are free.

options.t: It keeps all messages in RAM and flushes them to disk only in the background
options.why: Backwards — Kafka commits to disk and leans on the OS page cache. Its speed comes from sequential access patterns, not from avoiding disk.

options.t: It guarantees exactly-once delivery by default
options.why: The default is at-least-once. Exactly-once exists only for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines using transactions, and it's opt-in.

options.t: It sorts messages by priority
options.why: There is no priority concept. Records land in a partition in arrival order and stay in that order — position, not priority.

items.q: What is an offset in Kafka?

options.t: A record's monotonically increasing position within its own partition
options.why: Exactly. Offsets are positions, not IDs the system invents — which is why the broker needs no random-access ID index and consumers can resume by asking for a number.

options.t: A globally unique identifier assigned across the whole topic
options.why: Offsets are per-partition. Offset 500 exists in every partition and means a different record in each — a common confusion that breaks reasoning about ordering.

options.t: The byte position of the record in the segment file
options.why: Close but no — offsets are logical record positions. The .index file is what maps an offset to a byte position, and it does so only sparsely.

options.t: A timestamp in milliseconds
options.why: Timestamps exist separately, in the .timeindex. Offsets are counters, which is what makes 'resume from where I stopped' a single integer.

items.q: What is the ISR (in-sync replica set) for a partition?

options.t: Replicas, leader included, that are currently caught up
options.why: Yes — membership is dynamic, based on a lag-time threshold. A slow follower drops out and rejoins later, and that dynamism is the source of the most famous durability trap in the system.

options.t: All replicas configured for the partition
options.why: That's the replica set, which is fixed by the replication factor. The ISR is the subset currently keeping up, and it shrinks and grows on its own.

options.t: The replicas placed on the same rack or availability zone as the leader
options.why: Rack placement is a separate concern (spread replicas across failure domains). ISR membership is purely about how far behind a follower is.

options.t: The set of consumers currently reading the partition
options.why: Consumers aren't replicas. The ISR is a broker-side concept about copies of the log, not about who is reading it.

items.q: Why is the offset index sparse — roughly one entry per 4 KB of log — instead of one entry per record?

options.t: A dense index would be huge; sparse keeps it small, at the cost of a short scan
options.why: Right, and note what the trade buys: the scan is sequential from page cache, which is the operation this system is fastest at. Cheap index, cheap scan.

options.t: Because records are variable length, so an exact offset-to-byte mapping is impossible
options.why: Variable length is handled fine — batch headers carry sizes. Sparseness is a deliberate size-versus-scan trade, not a limitation.

options.t: To make compaction possible
options.why: Compaction is a separate mechanism that rewrites segments by key. It doesn't depend on the index being sparse.

options.t: So the index can be rebuilt quickly after a crash
options.why: A smaller index does rebuild faster, which is a nice side effect — but the reason is memory footprint on a multi-terabyte log.

items.q: With acks=1, what exactly can be lost?

options.t: Records the leader already acknowledged but had not yet shipped to followers
options.why: That is precisely the loss window. The producer was told 'yes', the new leader never saw those records, and nothing raises an error — silent loss.

options.t: Nothing — one acknowledgement is enough
options.why: One acknowledgement means one copy exists, on the machine that is about to fail. Durability comes from replication, and acks=1 doesn't wait for any.

options.t: Only records still sitting in the producer's buffer
options.why: Those are lost under any acks setting if the producer dies — that's not what distinguishes acks=1. The distinguishing loss is broker-side, after the ack.

options.t: The entire partition
options.why: Failover promotes a follower with most of the data. You lose the unreplicated tail, not the log.

items.q: When is log compaction the right retention policy instead of time-based deletion?

options.t: When the topic is really a table: current state per key
options.why: Yes. If a consumer rebuilding from offset 0 must end up with the latest value for every key, you can never delete the last record for a key, however old it is.

options.t: When the topic is very large
options.why: Size is what retention caps handle. Compaction is about the meaning of the data, not its volume — and compaction does real I/O, so it isn't a free size fix.

options.t: When consumers are slow
options.why: Slow consumers need a longer retention window, not compaction. Compaction would actually remove intermediate values a slow consumer never saw.

options.t: When records must never be deleted for regulatory reasons
options.why: Compaction does delete — it removes superseded values and, after a grace window, tombstoned keys. It keeps the latest per key, not everything.

items.q: Within one consumer group, how many members can read a single partition at the same time?

options.t: Exactly one
options.why: That's the rule that makes partitions the parallelism unit: a group can never have more useful members than the topic has partitions, and extras sit idle.

options.t: As many as you like — they coordinate via offsets
options.why: Offsets are committed per (group, partition), so two members on one partition would fight over one bookmark. The protocol assigns each partition to one member.

options.t: One per replica, so three at RF=3
options.why: Followers exist for durability, not for read scaling — all client traffic goes through the leader. Replication factor doesn't change consumer parallelism.

options.t: Two: one active and one standby
options.why: There is no standby-consumer concept in the group protocol. If a member dies, a rebalance hands its partitions to a survivor.

items.q: What is a leader epoch used for?

options.t: Fencing: any request stamped with an older epoch number is refused outright
options.why: Exactly chapter 2.3's fencing token, applied per partition. It also tells the returning replica where its epoch ended, so it truncates to the right point instead of guessing.

options.t: Measuring how long a broker has been the leader
options.why: It's a counter, not a clock — it increments on every leadership change. Its value is comparison, not duration.

options.t: Deciding how long segments are retained before deletion
options.why: Retention is driven by time and size settings. Epochs are about leadership identity during failover.

options.t: Ordering records within a partition
options.why: Offsets already order records. Epochs order leadership terms, which is a different problem — who is allowed to write at all.

items.q: Why do Kafka consumers pull from brokers instead of brokers pushing to consumers?

options.t: Consumers set their own pace, so backpressure is free
options.why: Right. A push broker would have to model every consumer's capacity and buffer for the slow ones; with pull, a struggling consumer just falls behind — and 'behind' is a number you can graph and alert on.

options.t: Pull consumes noticeably less network bandwidth across the cluster
options.why: Roughly the same bytes move either way, and idle pulling costs a little extra — which is why brokers hold fetch requests open (long polling) rather than answering 'nothing'.

options.t: Pull is required for TLS to work
options.why: Unrelated. TLS matters here for a different reason: it disables zero-copy transfer because encryption must happen in userspace.

options.t: Because brokers don't know which consumers exist
options.why: Brokers do know — the group coordinator tracks membership via heartbeats. Pull is a flow-control choice, not an information gap.

items.q: You size a cluster at 1 GB/sec ingress, 7-day retention, RF=3, and land on ~130 brokers. Each broker's NIC runs at about 3% utilization. What does that tell you?

options.t: Disk capacity binds, so retention is the biggest cost lever
options.why: The number produced a conclusion: cutting retention to 3 days roughly halves the fleet, while throughput doesn't move at all. That's estimation driving a decision — and it makes retention an owned policy, not a forgotten default.

options.t: The cluster is over-provisioned on brokers and should be shrunk
options.why: You can't shrink it — the disks are full of data you promised to keep. Broker count is set by bytes retained, not by NIC headroom.

options.t: You should increase the replication factor since there's spare network
options.why: RF=4 would add 33% more disk to a cluster already sized by disk. Spare network doesn't make spare disk, and RF=3 already survives one loss cleanly.

options.t: Compression should be turned off to save CPU
options.why: Exactly the wrong direction on a disk-bound cluster — compression is what shrinks the constraint that's actually binding.

items.q: A payments topic runs RF=3 with acks=all and no other durability settings. Two followers hit long GC pauses and drop out of the ISR. What is the producer's guarantee during that window?

options.t: Effectively acks=1: the ISR is now just the leader
options.why: This is the trap the whole crux exists for. acks=all is a promise about the ISR, and the ISR shrank. min.insync.replicas=2 fixes it by rejecting the write instead of making a false promise.

options.t: Unchanged — acks=all always waits for all three replicas
options.why: It waits for all replicas currently in sync, not all configured replicas. That distinction is exactly what cost Jepsen's test 520 of 987 acknowledged writes.

options.t: Writes are rejected automatically until the followers return
options.why: Only if you set min.insync.replicas. With no such setting the leader happily keeps acking alone — silence, not an error.

options.t: The partition goes offline
options.why: The leader is alive, so the partition serves normally. That's what makes the window dangerous: everything looks healthy while durability has quietly degraded.

items.q: Your consumer polls offsets 100-199, processes 100-149 (charging a card each), then the pod is killed before committing. What happens on restart?

options.t: Delivery resumes at 100, so 100-149 are processed a second time
options.why: That's the at-least-once duplicate window: everything between the last commit and the crash. The answer isn't to avoid it — it's idempotent consumers, so a repeat charge for the same order ID is a no-op.

options.t: Delivery resumes at 150 because the broker tracked what was delivered
options.why: Brokers don't track delivery — only committed offsets, and nothing was committed. Assuming the broker remembers is the single most common Kafka misconception.

options.t: The records are lost because the batch was abandoned
options.why: Nothing is lost — the log still holds every record and the committed offset is still 100. Loss would require committing before processing.

options.t: Kafka replays only 150-199
options.why: There's no per-record acknowledgement, so Kafka can't know 100-149 were done. Progress is one integer per partition, and that integer says 100.

items.q: A keyed topic partitioned by user_id has 12 partitions and needs more consumer parallelism. You raise it to 48. What just broke?

options.t: hash(key) mod N changed, so a user's events lose relative order
options.why: Right — repartitioning a keyed topic is a migration (chapter 2.11), not a config change. Any consumer rebuilding per-user state across the boundary sees events out of order, and there's no way to un-ring that bell.

options.t: Nothing — partition count can be raised freely
options.why: It can be raised freely on an unkeyed topic. On a keyed one, key stickiness is the guarantee you just voided, and the damage is permanent for events already written.

options.t: Retention resets and old data is deleted
options.why: Existing segments are untouched; old partitions keep their data. The breakage is about which partition future records go to.

options.t: Replication factor silently drops to 1 for the newly created partitions
options.why: New partitions inherit the topic's replication factor. Durability is fine — ordering is not.

items.q: A broker has 64 GB RAM. Your team proposes raising the JVM heap from 6 GB to 40 GB "so the broker can cache more messages." Your response?

options.t: Reject it: heap taken is page cache lost, plus longer GC pauses
options.why: Kafka's design deliberately avoids an in-process message cache to skip double buffering and keep GC cheap. A 40 GB heap shrinks the real cache and buys pauses long enough to look like broker failures.

options.t: Accept it — more heap always means more caching
options.why: There's nothing in the heap to cache. Message bytes go through page cache and, thanks to sendfile, often never enter the JVM at all.

options.t: Accept it, but only on the brokers that lead the hottest partitions
options.why: Selective wrongness is still wrong, and it makes the fleet inconsistent to operate. Hot partitions want more page cache, which means less heap, not more.

options.t: Raise it to 20 GB as a compromise
options.why: Splitting the difference on a decision that has a clear direction is how bad configs get shipped. Small heap, big page cache — and say why.

items.q: A producer sends a batch, the leader writes it, and the acknowledgement is lost on the network. The producer retries. What stops a duplicate?

options.t: The idempotent producer's sequence numbers let the broker drop it
options.why: Chapter 2.2's idempotency key, moved into the protocol. It also preserves ordering under retries — without it, a retried batch can land behind one that succeeded later.

options.t: Nothing — the duplicate is unavoidable and consumers must handle it
options.why: That was true before idempotent producers, and it's the reason they exist. Broker-side dedup closes this specific hole, though consumer-side duplicates from offset commits remain.

options.t: The broker deduplicates by comparing the contents of each record
options.why: Content hashing would be expensive and wrong — two genuinely identical events are legal. Dedup keys on producer identity and sequence, not payload.

options.t: Kafka transactions
options.why: Transactions give atomic visibility across partitions and build on idempotence, but they're a heavier tool. This hole is closed by sequence numbers alone.

items.q: A product manager asks for strict global ordering across a 1 GB/sec topic. What's the strongest response?

options.t: "Global order means one partition — one broker, one consumer, a hard throughput ceiling. You almost certainly want per-user ordering, which is free: key by user."
options.why: Names the real cost, then offers what they actually needed. Per-entity ordering costs nothing; total ordering costs the entire parallelism story of the system.

options.t: "Sure — I'll add sequence numbers and sort downstream."
options.why: Sorting a 1 GB/sec unbounded stream requires buffering until you're sure nothing earlier is coming, which needs a watermark and unbounded memory. This is a much harder problem wearing a casual answer.

options.t: "Kafka guarantees global ordering already."
options.why: It doesn't, and stating it confidently is a fast way to fail the round. Ordering is per-partition, always.

options.t: "Use one partition per consumer and merge by timestamp."
options.why: Producer clocks disagree and skew across machines, so timestamp merging produces plausible-looking wrong order. Ordering has to come from a single writer, not from clocks.

items.q: You're doing a rolling upgrade of 130 brokers. What gates each restart?

options.t: Wait for UnderReplicatedPartitions to return to 0
options.why: Restarting a second broker while partitions are still under-replicated can take out two of three replicas at once — a routine upgrade becomes an outage. The gate is a metric, not a stopwatch.

options.t: Wait five minutes between brokers
options.why: A timer is a guess about recovery that scales badly — re-replication time depends on how much data the broker held. Gate on the condition you actually care about.

options.t: Restart brokers in parallel within a rack to finish faster
options.why: Rack-aware placement puts replicas of the same partition in different racks, so a whole rack at once is precisely the correlated failure the placement exists to prevent.

options.t: Drain all consumers first
options.why: Consumers survive leadership moves by refreshing metadata and retrying. Draining them adds a rebalance storm to an already delicate operation.

items.q: A consumer group of 30 pods keeps stalling for 10-20 seconds at random. Logs show frequent rebalances. Most likely cause and fix?

options.t: Rebalance storms: members evicted for slow processing stall everyone
options.why: Classic rebalance storm: eager rebalancing stops everyone, the pause pushes another member past its deadline, and it cascades. Cooperative rebalancing only moves the partitions that must move.

options.t: The topic has too few partitions for the number of pods
options.why: Too few partitions means idle consumers, not periodic stalls for all of them. The symptom here is stop-the-world pauses, which points at the group protocol.

options.t: The brokers are running out of disk on their log directories
options.why: Disk pressure takes partitions offline and shows up as offline-partition and produce errors, not as group membership churn.

options.t: acks=all is slowing the producers, and the backlog stalls consumers downstream
options.why: That would show as produce latency. Consumer group stalls come from the coordinator and the rebalance protocol.

items.q: Interviewer: "Set unclean.leader.election.enable for this cluster. Go." Which answer reads most senior?

options.t: "Off for order and payment topics — data loss there is a lawsuit, an offline partition is a page. On for clickstream and metrics, where a gap in a graph beats blocking every producer. It's a per-topic classification, not a cluster switch."
options.why: Commits, gives the reason in business terms, and — the real signal — refuses the premise that this is one global setting. Classifying topics by what failure they can survive is the senior move.

options.t: "Off everywhere. Data loss is never acceptable."
options.why: Defensible and half-right, but absolute. It means a telemetry partition can block your entire producer fleet during an incident to protect data nobody would miss.

options.t: "On everywhere. Availability wins in a streaming system — Kafka is a transport rather than a system of record, so a handful of records missing after a bad failover is a far cheaper outcome than partitions sitting offline and blocking every producer in the fleet while someone hunts for a dead broker."
options.why: This is the setting that let Jepsen's test lose 520 acknowledged writes. Plenty of real systems of record ride on Kafka, and 'streams aren't important' is not a durability argument — length of explanation is not the same as strength of it.

options.t: "Whatever the default is — the defaults are well chosen."
options.why: The modern default (off) happens to be right, but deferring to it dodges the question being asked. The interviewer wants the trade-off reasoned, not delegated.

items.q: Ten minutes into "design Kafka," which agenda announcement shows you found the crux?

options.t: "Storage is a segment file and a sparse index — I'll sketch it fast. The real difficulty is replication: what counts as in-sync, what an ack promises, and how a stale leader is fenced. That's where I want most of our time."
options.why: Triages by difficulty, names the three mechanisms that every delivery guarantee reduces to, and claims the agenda. Everything else in Kafka is a well-chosen file format; this is the part that can silently lose data.

options.t: "I'd like to go deep on the exact record batch binary format and compression codecs."
options.why: Real knowledge, low signal. Format details are memorizable trivia; the interviewer is waiting to see whether you can reason about failure under partition.

options.t: "Let me spend the time on how we actually run this: StatefulSets so broker identity survives restarts, a persistent volume claim per broker, pod disruption budgets that stop the scheduler evicting two replicas of a partition at once, and a rolling-restart operator that gates on under-replicated partitions."
options.why: All real and all useful — and every word of it is packaging around the system rather than the system. Detail is not depth here: it skips the one thing only a distributed-systems answer can cover, which is what happens to acknowledged data when the network splits.

options.t: "The hard part is picking between Kafka, Pulsar, and Kinesis."
options.why: You were asked to build the thing, not shop for it. Comparison shopping instead of designing is a recognizable way to avoid the hard part.

items.q: Interviewer: "Traffic goes 10x — 10 GB/sec, same retention." Your 130 brokers become ~1,300. What's the strongest answer?

options.t: "One cluster that size is past comfortable — metadata, rebalances and blast radius all worsen together. I'd split by domain into several clusters, then add tiered storage so brokers are sized by throughput rather than retention, since our estimate showed we're disk-bound."
options.why: Names why scaling one cluster fails, gives two structural moves in priority order, and ties the second directly back to the binding constraint the estimate found. That last link is what separates a memorized answer from a reasoned one.

options.t: "It scales horizontally, so we add brokers."
options.why: Buzzword shield. It ignores that per-cluster metadata, failover time and blast radius all degrade as broker and partition counts climb — the very things 10x makes worse.

options.t: "Increase partition count 10x and move on."
options.why: You'll need more partitions, but that's a consequence, not a plan — and it makes the metadata problem worse while doing nothing about the petabytes on disk.

options.t: "I'd drop the replication factor to 2. That hands back a third of the disk immediately, which is exactly the constraint the estimate identified, and it absorbs most of the growth without buying a single extra machine or reshaping the cluster topology at all."
options.why: Paying for scale with durability, quietly, and dressing it up as an insight about the constraint. RF=2 with min.insync.replicas=2 means any single broker restart stops writes — a worse operational story at ten times the load.

items.q: A team asks you to guarantee exactly-once from Kafka into their Postgres inventory table. What do you commit to?

options.t: "Kafka transactions can't span Postgres. Take at-least-once and make the write idempotent — upsert keyed on the event ID — so redelivery is a no-op. If they need Postgres-to-Kafka atomicity, that's the outbox pattern."
options.why: Draws the boundary honestly: Kafka's exactly-once is Kafka-to-Kafka. Pushing dedup to the destination where the natural key lives is the design that actually holds, and naming the outbox for the reverse direction shows you know both directions.

options.t: "Enable transactions and read_committed — that gives exactly-once end to end."
options.why: A very common and very wrong claim. Commit markers make Kafka writes atomically visible to Kafka consumers; they say nothing about a database on the other side of a network call.

options.t: "I'd run two-phase commit between the consumer and Postgres, with a transaction coordinator that prepares both sides, collects the votes, and only then commits — that gives genuine atomicity across the two systems rather than an approximation of it."
options.why: Technically a real protocol, practically a coordinator that blocks every participant when it dies and a fragile dependency between two systems that should not share a fate (chapter 2.1). Idempotent upserts get the same outcome with none of the machinery.

options.t: "Have the consumer check whether the row exists before writing."
options.why: Check-then-write is a race the moment two consumers or a retry overlap. Let the database referee with a unique constraint and an upsert.

items.q: You may put ONE Kafka alert on the on-call pager. Which, and why?

options.t: Consumer lag, measured in time
options.why: Cluster-health metrics say whether the machine is well; lag says whether the promise is being kept, and it's the one number that catches broker problems, slow consumers and hot partitions alike. Measuring it in time is what makes it an SLO an engineer can act on.

options.t: Broker CPU above 80%
options.why: A high-CPU broker with everyone caught up is fine. This alert fires on states that don't hurt anyone and misses states that do.

options.t: Disk usage above 70%
options.why: It belongs on a dashboard with a slow-burn ticket, since retention makes disk growth predictable days ahead. Reserve the pager for something that's hurting users now.

options.t: Produce request rate dropping below a baseline
options.why: Traffic dips for a hundred harmless reasons, from a batch job finishing to a quiet Sunday. You'd train the on-call to ignore the pager, which costs more than the alert is worth.

items.q: Candidate A recites the full ISR/acks/epoch machinery flawlessly. Candidate B is rougher, but says: "I'll default to RF=3, acks=all, min.insync=2 with unclean election off for business topics — and my weak point is that this makes writes fail when two brokers are down, so I'd want a documented runbook for that state." Who grades higher?

options.t: B — a committed configuration with a named consequence is ownership
options.why: B chose a default, priced it, and volunteered the failure it creates before being asked. A knows the mechanism; B has decided how to run it — and interviewers grade the second.

options.t: A — complete and accurate coverage of the mechanisms is the foundation of the grade
options.why: Accuracy is table stakes at senior. Reciting mechanisms without picking settings reads as a well-read engineer who hasn't operated one.

options.t: Equal — B's answer is a subset of A's knowledge
options.why: It's a subset of the facts and a superset of the judgment. The rubric grades decisions made and costs acknowledged, not surface area covered.

options.t: B, but only for the honesty about the weakness
options.why: Partial credit. The self-critique matters as evidence of someone who imagines their system failing — but the commitment plus the reason is what does the real work.

items.q: One group is 4 hours behind on a topic taking 200 MB/sec. Producers for unrelated topics on the same brokers suddenly get slower too. Diagnose it.

options.t: The backlog is far past the page-cache window, so catch-up reads come off disk and contend with the write path on the same brokers
options.why: This is why the page-cache calculation earns its place: lag past ~38 minutes converts a freshness problem into a cluster-wide performance problem. Mitigations are a consumer quota to cap the bleeding, or a business decision to skip ahead if the data is disposable.

options.t: The lagging group is holding a lock other producers wait on
options.why: There is no such lock — producers append to leaders and consumers read independently. Contention here is physical (disk and I/O bandwidth), not logical.

options.t: Rebalances in the lagging group are blocking producers
options.why: Rebalances stall that group's consumption only; they never touch the produce path. Cross-topic impact points at a shared physical resource.

options.t: The leader for those partitions moved, so producers are retrying
options.why: Leadership moves cause a brief blip and a metadata refresh, not a sustained slowdown correlated with someone else's backlog.
